query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled substrate pre‐heating step during selective laser melting (SLM) of high-entropy alloys will improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by reducing thermal gradients, residual stresses, and fabrication-induced defects via a more uniform solidification process.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components produced under standard SLM conditions (without pre-heating) that typically exhibit high thermal gradients, residual stresses, and defects such as porosity and microcracking.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized substrate pre-heating protocol to elevate the build platform temperature during the SLM process.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be implemented during SLM processing for high-entropy alloys under otherwise standard laser power, scan speed, and atmosphere conditions; the target pre-heating temperature should be in a moderately elevated range based on the specific alloy system.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradient between the melt pool and surrounding material, resulting in a more uniform solidification rate, decreased residual stress accumulation, and a refined microstructure with lower porosity and fewer unwanted phase segregations.
generation.mechanism: By pre-heating the substrate, the temperature difference between the molten region and the base is decreased, which moderates the cooling rate, reduces thermal shock and contraction upon solidification, limits the formation of internal stress concentrations, and lowers the occurrence of gas entrapment or liquation-related defects that compromise dimensional accuracy and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to components fabricated without substrate pre-heating, pre-heated builds will display enhanced dimensional precision (lower distortions and improved geometric accuracy), higher mechanical strength (e.g., increased yield strength and tensile strength), and a lower density of defects (reduced porosity and microcracking).
generation.baseline: As-built HEA components produced by SLM at room temperature without pre-heating, which have demonstrated challenges related to high residual stress, dimensional inaccuracy, and fabrication-induced defects.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the pre-heating intervention is expected to hold for SLM-fabricated high-entropy alloys under conditions where laser parameters and powder characteristics remain consistent; outcomes in other AM technologies or drastically different processing environments may not directly apply.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal pre-heating temperature and its precise impact may vary depending on the specific HEA composition and process parameters; further experimental titration will be required to quantify the effect size and to ensure that elevated temperatures do not introduce new issues such as undesirable phase transformations.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy components by SLM under identical laser power, scanning strategies, and powder parameters, differing only in the substrate temperature—one group with standard room temperature conditions (control) and one group with the optimized pre-heating regime. After fabrication, use high-precision 3D metrology to assess dimensional accuracy, quantitative image analysis (e.g., SEM) to measure defect density, and mechanical testing (tensile, hardness) to evaluate mechanical integrity.
measurements: Residual stress levels (via X-ray diffraction or similar methods)
Defect density and porosity percentage (using microscopy and image analysis)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-heated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in dimensional accuracy, lower defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to control samples, then the hypothesis that substrate pre-heating improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity is falsified.

This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.

AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) possesses excellent properties including exceptional strength–ductility synergy, high corrosion resistance, and good thermal stability. Selective laser melting (SLM) additive manufacturing facilitates the convenient fabrication of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA parts with complex geometries. Here, the SLM process optimization was conducted to achieve a high relative density of as-built CoCrFeNiMn HEA bulks. The mechanisms of process-induced defects and process control were elucidated. The microscale mechanical behaviors were analyzed through in situ scanning electron microscopy observation during the compression tests on micro-pillars of the as-built HEA. The stress–strain characteristics by repeated slip and mechanism of “dislocation avalanche” during the compression of micro-pillars were discussed. The high-cycle fatigue tests of the as-built HEA were performed. It was found that a large number of nano-twins were induced by the fatigue, causing a non-negligible cycle softening phenomenon.
